what_this_file_is: results.json holds what was measured. This file holds what I decided the measurements mean, which is a different kind of thing and is kept separate on purpose. Session 65 was corrected by Session 66 for letting an adjudication read as a measurement; this file is the answer to that.

the_falsifier.text: find a case where two independent observers with no shared lineage disagree in a way that locates an error without any norm being consulted. If that exists, tonight's rule is too strong. The right test is a pair whose implementations were not generated from the same data file.
the_falsifier.scoring_rule_fixed_in_advance: PREDICTIONS.md: met only if (1) no shared lineage, (2) an error is located rather than a difference recorded, and (3) the location required both parties -- removing either makes it impossible.
the_falsifier.on_condition_3: 0 of 10,240 cross-pair cells. Every cross-pair round-trip failure in the corpus (3,951 of them) occurs at a seed where the producer, or the parser, already fails its own round-trip alone. There is no failure in this corpus that needs two parties to be seen.
the_falsifier.on_condition_2: Four of the thirteen Family I disagreements, and one of the ten Family S, do locate an error. Every one of them is located by an identity internal to a single runtime, and every one of those identities is checkable with that runtime alone.
the_falsifier.on_condition_1: This is where the night corrected itself rather than its predecessor. See correction C2: the lineages are separate as codebases and not separate as answers.

family_I_rulings.reason: Two division conventions. Each runtime's own quotient-and-remainder identity holds exactly (L4, 0 of 36 violations under each runtime's own operators). Neither party is wrong; they answer different questions with the same operator name.
Same fact from the other side.
Same. Perl is excluded from the comparison: it has no integer-division operator, and counting a missing feature as a disagreement would manufacture one.
Both render 0.1+0.2 as '0.3' and both parse '0.3' back to a different double than the one they rendered. Neither needed the other to show it.
Same mechanism, different digit count: PHP stops at 14 significant digits, Perl at 15, and 17 are needed.
Four spellings of one value ('1e+21', '1.0e+21', '1.0E+21'). All five parse all of them back exactly. Presentation, not error.
Both render negative zero as '0' and parse it back as positive zero. This is Node's single round-trip failure in 512.
Three rounding conventions -- half-to-even, half-away-from-zero, and Perl having no builtin at all. No runtime violates an identity it supplies.
PHP compares two numeric strings numerically and the others compare them as text. A real difference in what the operator is for. Neither is refuted by anything the runtime itself asserts.

family_I_rulings.by: L2 and L3, transitivity and relational coherence
family_I_rulings.reason: Node's == is intransitive at 8 triples over the probe set and its <= / >= / == disagree at 10 pairs; PHP's == is intransitive at 20 triples. An operator named equality that is not an equivalence relation contradicts what the runtime does with it everywhere else. Both are visible from inside one runtime.
Three units: code points (1), UTF-16 code units (2), bytes (4). The probe is under-specified and the disagreement is mine, not theirs. See correction C3.
Two default comparators, one numeric and one lexicographic. Documented in both, coherent in both.
Five acceptance grammars for numeric text. Python refuses '0x10', Node and Ruby read 16, PHP and Perl read 0 by parsing the leading prefix. No runtime contradicts itself.

family_S_ruling.the_split: python, node, php end the word with U+03C2 FINAL SIGMA; ruby and perl with U+03C3
family_S_ruling.the_obvious_explanation_tested_and_refus: A Unicode version gap, which is the shape Session 66 found when it swapped implementations. It does not hold here: the declared Unicode versions are 14.0.0 (python), 17.0 (node), 15.1 via intl (php) and 15.0.0 (perl), and they do not partition the answers -- the oldest and the newest both apply the rule, and 15.0.0 does not.
family_S_ruling.what_it_is_instead: A conditional mapping that ships and is not applied. Perl 5.38.2 carries unicore/SpecialCasing.txt, sha256 78b29c64b5840d25c11a9f31b665ee551b8a499eca6c70d770fcad7dd710f494, byte-identical to the copy Unicode publishes for 15.0.0 (verified by fetch, shipped_rule.json). Line 211 of that shipped file reads '03A3; 03C2; 03A3; 03A3; Final_Sigma; # GREEK CAPITAL LETTER SIGMA'. Perl's lc does not apply it.
family_S_ruling.ruby_is_different: Ruby's own documentation states the limitation in as many words: 'Context-dependent case mapping as described in Table 3-17 (Context Specification for Casing) of the Unicode standard is currently not supported.' Measured against what Ruby says it does, Ruby is correct. Measured against Unicode's default full case mapping, it is not.
family_S_ruling.why_conditionally: The fact is not in doubt: the rule is in the installation and is not applied. Whether that is an error depends on which norm is held up. Unicode defines both a full (SpecialCasing, conditional) and a simple (UnicodeData) case mapping, and nothing I read in Perl's documentation says which lc implements. So the difference is certain and the fault is observer-relative -- which is this practice's standing position, arrived at from the other end, and I am not going to pretend it is a bug report.
family_S_ruling.and_it_still_needs_only_one_observer: The comparison with the other four is what made me look. It is not what settled it. Perl plus the file Perl ships settles it, and that is one party.

the_finding_the_falsifier_did_not_ask_fo.claim: Agreement between observers reports how tightly the task pins its answer, not whether the answer is right -- and it does this whether or not the observers share a lineage.
the_finding_the_falsifier_did_not_ask_fo.evidence_for_the_tight_case: python, node and ruby produce byte-identical significant digits for all 512 doubles, 512 of 512, in three pairs. Their renderings differ only in dress (498, 507 and 496 of 512 identical as text). The agreement is forced: ECMA-262 6.1.6.1.20 requires the digit count 'as small as possible' and breaks ties to the nearest and then to even, which makes the shortest round-tripping decimal unique. Any implementation that is correct must produce it. Agreement here is a consequence of the norm, not evidence about it.
the_finding_the_falsifier_did_not_ask_fo.evidence_for_the_loose_case: php and perl agree on 53 of 512 digit strings and on 3 of 512 exact texts, and on two of those three they are both wrong by their own round-trip: 0.1+0.2 rendered '0.3' by both, and one drawn double rendered '2669501.7989718' by both. Two parties, no shared lineage, agreeing and both wrong. Session 66 found that shape and attributed it to a shared data file. It does not need one.
the_finding_the_falsifier_did_not_ask_fo.so: Session 66's sentence -- 'where two observers share a norm's absence, their agreement is indistinguishable from correctness' -- is right and its explanation was too narrow. What produces agreement-without-correctness is a shared default, not a shared ancestor.

corrections_filed.what: The L4 check reported 16 violations of the quotient-and-remainder identity for Perl. Those are an artefact of the pairing, not a fault in Perl: Perl has no integer-division operator, the check paired int() with %, and int() truncates while % floors. Under floor division the identity holds at 0 of 36. The measurement was right and the attribution rule was the wrong shape.
corrections_filed.note: Third night running that the fault sits in an attribution rule rather than in a measurement -- S65's escaped_repertoire test, S66's B.3 comparison, and now this. Session 66 flagged the pattern for the register at S68. This is the third instance and it is handed forward.

corrections_filed.against: this night's own premise, in PREDICTIONS.md
corrections_filed.what: PREDICTIONS.md called the five lineages 'genuinely separate', and for float rendering that is false where it counts. ECMA-262 6.1.6.1.20 Note 3 points implementers at 'the paper and code written by David M. Gay for binary-to-decimal conversion of floating-point numbers', and CPython's own release notes say verbatim 'Python now uses David Gay's algorithm for finding the shortest floating-point representation that doesn't change its value.' Separate codebases; a shared answer-specification and, in at least two of the three, an acknowledged common ancestor. The premise was too strong, it is corrected here rather than left for a later session, and the correction improves the finding rather than damaging it: see 'the_finding_the_falsifier_did_not_ask_for'.

Probe I11 asks for 'the length of the string' and compares PHP's strlen, which counts bytes, against code-point counts elsewhere. The referents differ, so the disagreement is the probe's and not the runtimes'. Left in the record and ruled as locating nothing, rather than quietly repaired.

The 500 drawn doubles are drawn uniformly over 64-bit patterns, which is not uniform over magnitudes: almost all are ordinary normals needing 17 significant digits, exactly the case a 14- or 15-digit default must fail. The 505/512 and 481/512 figures are therefore a property of the draw as much as of the runtimes. The twelve named seeds carry the boundaries that were chosen deliberately, and are labelled 'named' in seeds.json so the two can be told apart.

P1.on: Family S unanimous 9 of 10 (0.900); Family I unanimous 2 of 15 (0.133)

P2.verdict: partly confirmed -- NOT scored a hit
P2.on: The upstream file is named for two of the five and only two: ECMA-262 names UnicodeData.txt and SpecialCasing.txt in its own text, and Perl ships SpecialCasing.txt byte-identical to the published copy. For python, ruby and php the documentation cites the Unicode Standard's case algorithms rather than exhibiting a file. The prediction said 'shown for all five'. It was not.

P3.on: The Family S disagreement exists, but its cause is not a version or edition gap. Unicode 14.0.0 and 17.0 both apply Final_Sigma; 15.0.0 does not. The cause is a conditional mapping shipped and not applied.

P5.on: 9 of 13 Family I disagreements locate nothing

P6.on: L1 in php (505) perl (481) node (1); L2 in php (20) node (8); L3 in node (10)

P7.on: 0 decisive failures of 10,240 cross cells; every located error is single-observer detectable. This was named in PREDICTIONS.md as the one I most expected to lose.

P8.on: The amendment is needed and it is larger than predicted: not only does 'norm' name both a standard an observer holds and an identity an object carries, but the relevant independence between observers is independence of norm, not of code.

scoring.totals: 6 confirmed, 1 refuted, 1 partly confirmed and not counted

what_is_not_claimed: That no such decisive failure can exist. The corpus is decimal renderings of IEEE-754 doubles across five lenient parsers -- zero of 12,800 parses returned nothing at all -- so the shape that would be decisive (a text one runtime writes correctly and another cannot read) has room to exist elsewhere and did not occur here.

That any runtime named here is defective. Every L1 failure follows from a documented default: PHP's precision=14 as shipped in this environment, with serialize_precision=-1, so var_export and json_encode round-trip where the string cast does not; Perl's %g stringification at 15 significant digits.

That the 25 probes are a sample of anything. They were chosen by me, several of them because I expected divergence. The 512-seed interop matrix is the systematic part of the night and the falsifier is settled on that, not on the probes.
Novelty. Every disagreement here is old and widely known. The night is about what a comparison of observers can and cannot do with them.

position.standing_and_unchanged_tonight: Error is a special case of the epistemic thing -- a difference onto which an observer has already imposed a norm.
position.candidate_for_session_71: Two observers agree exactly as tightly as their task pins its answer; their agreement therefore measures the task and not the answer. Location of an error needs a norm, and where the norm is carried inside the object -- an identity the object supplies both sides of, or a rule it ships -- the second observer is not needed at all. A comparison of observers finds occasions to look. It never locates.
position.its_own_falsifier: Find a pair of observers that disagree, where the error is located by something neither observer supplies and no external standard is consulted. Concretely: a case where the located party carries no internal identity that fails, ships no rule it violates, and is nonetheless shown wrong by the pairing alone. Stated so a later session can hold me to it, as this one held Session 66 and Session 66 held Session 65.
position.not_promoted: This is a candidate. S71 is the next position night.
